item.title: Turning off radiators in empty rooms actually increases heating costs
item.description: Many people turn off radiators in guest rooms, home offices or utility rooms to save energy, but according to French agency ADEME, this backfires. Cold air is heavier and seeps under doors and through walls into heated rooms, causing them to cool faster. Radiators elsewhere must work harder, putting greater strain on the heating system. item.title: Keeping spiders in your home this autumn is a good idea
item.description: Spiders in your home form a natural trap for pests. Their daily menu consists precisely of the intruders that disturb our nights and daily lives. item.description: In 2021, around 1,000 Swiss citizens received two pairs of white cotton underwear in the mail to bury, as part of the citizen science project 'Proof by Underpants' run by the University of Zurich and Agroscope. item.description: In April 2021, a man approaching 80 knocked on the door of Delmar College of Hair & Esthetics in Red Deer, Alberta. item.title: Biologist hears a barnacle click at low tide
item.description: Phil Starks, professor of biology at Tufts University, describes how he heard a barnacle clicking and snapping at low tide on Tongue Point. This led him to reflect on how careful observation and listening to nature can reveal hidden animal behavior. item.title: Viagra-like pill slows cognitive decline in Alzheimer's
item.description: A new pill called AR1001, developed by South Korean company AriBio, slowed cognitive decline in people with early Alzheimer's by 31 percent over one year, according to phase 3 results presented at a conference in Boston. The drug belongs to the same medication family as Viagra and works by improving blood flow to the brain. Experts say it is remarkable...

item.title: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
item.description: On November 24, 167 years ago, British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, in which he set out his theory of evolution. The first edition has been hailed by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written. item.description: One of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, the Riemann hypothesis, appears to have finally been proven after more than a century. item.description: Forty-six years ago, Carl Sagan, a renowned science communicator and researcher of extraterrestrial life, explained the fourth dimension in an understandable way in episode 10 of the 1980 PBS series „Cosmos". item.description: In Gainesville, Florida, Sighle Williams worked at Mac's Drive Thru for 37 years, where she was known for her warmth and her ability to remember every customer and their order. item.title: Ella Fitzgerald forgets lyrics and wins Grammy
item.description: On February 13, 1960, Ella Fitzgerald took the stage in Berlin to sing 'Mack the Knife'. Halfway through the number, she completely forgot the lyrics. item.title: Automatic pardons clear criminal records for abortion in England and Wales
item.description: Women in England and Wales who were ever arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancy now have no criminal record on that matter. Since 16 November, police and courts must automatically delete this data without the women having to take any action themselves. item.title: New thumb implant relieves arthritis without bone removal
item.description: A new thumb prosthesis, the CMC Touch 1, offers a solution for people with advanced arthritis of the thumb (carpometacarpal arthritis). The Swiss implant, developed by KeriMedical, functions as a ball joint that replaces the worn saddle joint without requiring removal of the trapezium bone. item.title: Son tracks down writers of comfort letters to wounded Vietnam veteran
item.description: In 1967, 33 schoolchildren from Massachusetts wrote letters to an unknown, wounded Marine in Vietnam. HM3 Russell Jacobson lay in an understaffed hospital with 12 gunshot wounds and shrapnel fragments, refused food and could not speak for weeks. item.title: Whale genome decoded using drone and whale snot
item.description: Scientists have for the first time mapped a whale's complete genome using snot. Marine mammal ecologist Éadin O'Mahony and colleagues used small commercial drones with sterile petri dishes attached to capture the exhaled water vapor from whales.
